hero.name: Dinesh
hero.who: a 36-year-old AC repair contractor in Chennai whose skilled team keeps making silly slips

story.b: Dinesh has repaired air conditioners in Chennai for fifteen years, and he now runs a small team of four technicians from a shop in Velachery. Everyone says he is one of the best in the area. So the call from a customer in Adyar hurts. Two days after his team installed a new split AC, water is dripping onto her new wooden floor. The drain pipe was never tightened. The week before, a technician forgot to check the voltage before switching on a unit, and a fuse blew. Nobody on his team is careless. They all know these steps by heart. Dinesh rides home on his scooter, angry and puzzled, wondering how such good people keep missing such simple things.

ask.q: Dinesh's skilled team keeps missing simple steps they already know. What is most likely going wrong?
o: They need more training on how air conditioners work
They know what to do but forget basic steps under pressure
He hired the wrong people and should replace them
ask.why: His technicians clearly know the job, so more training will not fix it, and replacing good people wastes real skill. The trouble is the most common kind of failure: knowing exactly what to do and still forgetting it in the rush of a busy day.

chapters.take: Most mistakes come from forgetting what we know, not from not knowing.

story.b: On Sunday, Dinesh writes every mistake from the last two months on the small whiteboard at the back of the shop. Then he draws a line down the middle. On the left go mistakes made because nobody knew the answer. On the right go mistakes made because someone forgot. The left side has just one entry: a new inverter model that showed an error code none of them had seen. The right side keeps growing. Drain pipe not tightened. Voltage not checked. Customer not shown how to clean the filter. Remote batteries forgotten. Dinesh stares at it for a long time. His team does not need to know more. They need help remembering what they already know.

ask.q: Dinesh sees that almost every mistake is in the forgot column. What does that tell him to work on?
o: Helping his team reliably do the steps they already know
Sending everyone on a long technical course
Focusing only on the strange new error code
ask.why: Two kinds of failure need different fixes. Not knowing calls for learning, but forgetting calls for a way to catch slips. With nearly every mistake on the forgetting side, a course or a focus on the one rare puzzle would miss the real problem.

chapters.take: Ask whether a mistake came from not knowing or from forgetting. The fix is different.

story.b: Dinesh spends a day riding along with his team to see what really happens. By noon they have finished three jobs across the city. It is thirty-eight degrees on the terraces where the outdoor units sit. Customers call constantly with questions. A building watchman makes them wait twenty minutes for the lift. Between jobs they eat curd rice standing up. By the fourth job, even Dinesh catches himself about to leave without testing the cooling. That evening he writes a list of key steps for every installation, prints it on a card and slips one into each tool bag. Selvi, the newest technician, says she can remember everything if she just concentrates harder.

ask.q: Selvi says a list is unnecessary because she can remember everything by concentrating. What should Dinesh tell her?
o: She is right, so the card is only for slower workers
Concentrating harder is the answer, so she should rest more and focus
Even experts get tired and interrupted, so a written list catches what memory drops
ask.why: Hot, busy, interrupted days overload anyone's memory, however skilled. A simple list is not a sign of weakness. It catches the steps a tired brain skips. Treating it as only for slow workers, or relying on concentration, leaves the same gaps open.

chapters.take: Memory slips under pressure. A simple written list does not.

story.b: After two weeks, Dinesh checks the tool bags. The cards are there, crumpled and clean, clearly unread. He looks at his list again. Twenty-eight steps, including obvious ones like switching off the power and unpacking the unit. No wonder nobody reads it. He sits with a red pen and keeps only the steps people actually forget. Drain pipe tight. Voltage checked. Cooling tested for ten minutes. Filter cleaning shown to customer. Area cleaned. Remote working. Bill explained. Seven lines, in plain Tamil and English. He also changes how it is used. The team works from memory as usual, then pauses at the door for one minute and confirms each line before leaving.

ask.q: Nobody uses Dinesh's twenty-eight-step card. How should he fix it?
o: Make it even more detailed so nothing is left out
Cut it to the few critical steps people miss and check them in a quick pause
Laminate it in bright colours so people notice it
ask.why: Long lists get ignored, especially when they include steps nobody ever forgets. A short card with only the commonly missed steps can be checked in a minute at the door. More detail makes it heavier, and bright colours do not change what is inside.

chapters.take: A good checklist is short, plain and covers only what people forget.

story.h: Five minutes before the big job
story.b: Dinesh wins his biggest contract yet: twenty units for a new software office on the IT corridor. On the first morning, his team, an electrician from another firm and the building's facilities manager all arrive together. Usually everyone would just start working. Instead Dinesh gathers them near the lift for five minutes. Each person says their name, their job that day and one thing that worries them. Selvi mentions that a wall on the third floor looks too thin for heavy brackets. The electrician admits two power points are not ready yet. The facilities manager says the false ceiling goes up on Thursday. In five minutes, three problems that could have cost a week are out in the open.

ask.q: Dinesh's next big site involves three different teams. How should he start the first morning?
o: Hold a short huddle where everyone states their role and one risk
Let everyone begin right away to save time
Send a long email with all the instructions the night before
ask.why: A quick huddle makes people speak, so worries come out before work starts and everyone knows who does what. Starting straight away saves five minutes but risks days of rework. A long email goes one way, and nobody gets the chance to raise a problem.

chapters.take: Some of the best checklists simply make sure everyone speaks before work begins.

story.b: Ravi has been with Dinesh for twelve years and is the fastest technician on the team. He refuses to use the door card. He says he has done thousands of installations and does not need a list to tell him how. Dinesh understands the feeling. He felt it too at first. So he stops arguing and simply uses the card himself on every job, out loud, in front of everyone. On Friday, at a flat in Anna Nagar, he asks Ravi to check his work against the card. Ravi finds that Dinesh forgot to show the customer the filter. They both laugh. The next morning, Dinesh notices a card in Ravi's shirt pocket.

ask.q: Ravi, the most skilled technician, feels insulted by the checklist. What will most likely win him over?
o: Order him to use it or face a pay cut
Let him skip it since he is the best
Use it openly himself and invite others to check his own work
ask.why: Skilled people often feel a checklist questions their talent. When the boss uses it openly and lets it catch his own slip, it becomes a mark of professionals, not beginners. Threats create resentment, and letting the best person skip it tells everyone the list is optional.

chapters.take: Real professionals accept they are human and check their work anyway.

story.h: A quiet season at the shop
story.b: Two months later, the summer rush is over and something unusual has happened. Not one customer has called Dinesh about a leak. The cards in the tool bags are bent and stained with tea now, which makes him happy, because it means they are being used. The IT corridor job finished two days early. Before every big site, the team still gathers for its five-minute huddle, and the electricians from the other firm have started asking for it. Ravi has even suggested adding one line to the card, about checking that the outdoor unit is properly bolted down. Dinesh adds it gladly. The forgot column on the whiteboard is almost empty now.

chapters.take: Skill gets you far. A simple check makes sure it gets you there every time.
